..
Wednesday through Thursday: An upper low off the northern British
Columbia coast is ushering impulses into the PNW. The low is 
too far north to result in precipitation, but it will bring 
variably cloudy skies. A weak front passage will bring a little
bit of breeziness, over the Spokane Area, Upper Columbia Basin
to Moses Lake into the Okanogan Valley. Gusts of 15-20 mph are
possible. Highs will be near seasonal normals, reaching the 
lower to mid 70s,

On Thursday, a trough will start to dig down from the Gulf of 
Alaska, bringing southwesterly flow over the forecast area. This
will result in higher heights briefly brushing the area as a 
broad ridge sets up in the central US. Temperatures will briefly
rise back into the high 70s and low 80s. 

Thursday night through Sunday: This trough strengthens Thursday
night and moves south to PNW coast. Rain chances increase over 
the Cascades Thursday evening, becoming likely there overnight 
while chances expand into central WA. Friday the leading strong
cold front pushes across eastern WA and ID early in the day,
with the parent low tracking across the area. This will bring 
widespread rain, gusty winds, and chances for afternoon and 
evening thunderstorms. Models continue to diverge on the speed 
and track of the low. The system moves out of the area by 
Saturday night per most guidance, though the ECMWF has a slower 
solution with precipitation lingering in the northern mountains 
and ID Panhandle through early Sunday morning. 


* Precipitation amounts: the NBM show the 24-hour probability 
  of wetting rains (>=0.10") around 50-90%. Those probabilities 
  rose about 30-50% over the past couple days. The deeper 
  Columbia Basin and L-C Valley have the lowest risk. Areas that
  will see the highest rainfall include the Cascades, northern 
  mountains, Idaho Panhandle; rain amounts between 0.25 to 0.50"
  are forecast; with localized total between 0.75-1" possible 
  near the Cascade crest and northern mountains. Snow amounts 
  have stayed similar, with the 6000-7000 feet and above in the 
  Cascades having a chance to see a couple inches of snow. 
  Elevations 5000 feet and above look to see under an inch of 
  snow. Any travelers or hikers anticipating being in those 
  higher elevations this weekend should pay close attention to 
  the forecast over the next few days. 

 * Thunderstorms: the timing of the front and low passing
   through will be during peak daytime heating hours, and
   cooling air aloft will result in steep lapse rates. Forcing
   associated with the trough combined with these steep lapse
   rates and a couple hundred joules of SBCAPE will support the
   chances for thunderstorms Friday afternoon and evening. Areas
   from Moses Lake to Spokane and northward have a 15 to 25
   percent chance of thunderstorms, with the rest of the
   forecast area seeing around 10 percent. This environment also
   points to the potential for enhanced outflow winds with these
   thunderstorms, which will be tapping into some stronger
   environmental winds. See below for more about general winds.

 * Winds: There remains notable differences as to how quickly
   winds increase and how strong winds will be Friday and what
   areas of the CWA will see the highest winds. The various
   models have a differing ideas. However, I believe there could
   be a couple distinct areas of enhanced wind: (1) in the
   morning with the frontal passage and (2) in the afternoon to
   evening with the mixing and upper low. Overall confidence
   leans to winds being strongest in the afternoon and early
   evening, then gradually decline overnight. Areas forecast to
   see the highest wind gusts are from the Waterville Plateau
   and Columbia Basin and West Plains area, with gusts averaging
   25-35 mph. The NBM sometimes underforecast winds around the
   Palouse, so this area may be included in that area and the
   forecast does not go straight NBM for that reason. The NBM
   even gives a 40 to 70% chance of wind gusts near 40 mph over
   the Waterville Plateau and Upper Columbia Basin and a 25-40%
   chance of wind gusts near 50 mph. Elsewhere wind gusts of 
   15-25 mph are forecast. Yet there is the potential for winds 
   to be stronger in the morning with the cold front passage 
   than currently forecast.

Overall confidence is high in rain and winds Friday, with 
moderate confidence in thunderstorms. Lower confidence exists, 
however, with regard to the wind strength. Depending on how 
strong the winds are it could have more or less impacts. As this
forecast period enters the scope the short-term and higher 
resolution models, I think confidence will increase. But impacts
are possible, including airborne objects, difficult travel for 
high profile vehicles, maybe some blowing dust. The stronger 
wind scenarios could also lead to localized power outages. 
/AS/Solveig
